q: A developer committed an AWS access key in config/settings.py, pushed to GitLab and immediately deleted it in the next commit. What is the FIRST step?
options: Rewrite history with git filter-repo and force push
Add the finding's fingerprint to .gitleaksignore
Deactivate the key in IAM (aws iam update-access-key --status Inactive)
Create a new repo without the old history
explain: The secret is compromised from the moment of the push, and deleting or rewriting history doesn't undo copies that have already been made. First the key is deactivated, followed by rotation, investigation and only then possibly cleaning up history. .gitleaksignore without revocation only hides the problem.

q: You run gitleaks dir . over /root/kurs-shop and don't see the AWS key you know leaked in the commit "Početna verzija API-ja". Why?
options: gitleaks doesn't recognize AWS keys without .gitleaks.toml
gitleaks dir scans only the current files on disk; the key is in the history, so you need gitleaks git
--redact is missing
You need to add --log-opts="--all" to dir
explain: dir (files) looks at files as they are now, and the key was removed by a later commit. gitleaks git reads the history via git log -p. The default rules cover AWS, --redact only hides the value, and --log-opts applies to the git subcommand, not to dir.

q: An old pipeline calls gitleaks detect --source . -v and developers ask whether that's correct for gitleaks 8.30. What is the correct modern equivalent?
options: gitleaks scan --git .
gitleaks protect --staged
trufflehog git file://.
gitleaks git . -v
explain: Since 8.19, detect and protect are deprecated (they work, but are hidden); scanning history is gitleaks git, and files gitleaks dir. protect --staged is the old pre-commit way, the scan subcommand doesn't exist, and TruffleHog is a different tool.

q: The secret detection job prints the full values of found tokens in the CI log. What do you add to the command gitleaks git . -v?
options: --redact
--no-banner
--exit-code 0
--report-format sarif
explain: --redact replaces the secret's value in the output and the report (optionally a percentage, e.g. --redact=50). --no-banner only removes the logo, --exit-code 0 would disable the gate, and the report format doesn't affect what is printed in the log.

q: kurs-shop's internal tokens have the format kshop_ followed by 32 lowercase alphanumeric characters. The default rules don't catch them. How do you add them while keeping all the built-in rules?
options: In .gitleaks.toml you create [[rules]] with regex kshop_[a-z0-9]{32}, without [extend]
In .gitleaksignore you add the line kshop_*
In .gitleaks.toml you put [extend] useDefault = true and add [[rules]] with id, regex and keywords = ["kshop_"]
You run gitleaks git --enable-rule kshop
explain: [extend] useDefault = true keeps the built-in rules, and [[rules]] adds a new one; keywords speed up the scan. Without [extend], your own configuration replaces the default one, .gitleaksignore is for exceptions, and --enable-rule only selects existing rules by ID.

q: The security team has 300 findings from scanning all repos and wants to deal first with secrets that are actually active. Which tool and option most directly give that list?
options: gitleaks git --baseline-path
TruffleHog with --results=verified
gitleaks dir --max-target-megabytes 1
TruffleHog with --no-verification
explain: TruffleHog verifies a secret against the vendor's API and with --results=verified shows only confirmed active ones. gitleaks has no verification; a baseline only hides old findings, and --no-verification disables exactly what you need.

q: In an MR pipeline, a job runs trufflehog git file://. --since-commit main --branch HEAD --results=verified,unknown --fail. The job ends with exit code 183. What does that mean?
options: TruffleHog found results that match the --results filter
The git clone failed because GIT_DEPTH isn't 0
Verification failed because of the network
TruffleHog couldn't update itself
explain: With --fail, TruffleHog returns 183 when there are results; 0 means no findings, and 1 that an error occurred. Failed verification gives the finding an unknown status, not a separate exit code.

q: Match the task with the command that accomplishes it in the lab (without network access).
options: Scan staged changes in a pre-commit hook
Scan the entire kurs-shop git history with TruffleHog
Produce a SARIF report for the history
Test a new rule against a single string
explain: The hook uses git --pre-commit --staged, TruffleHog reads the local repo via a file:// URL without verification because there is no network, SARIF comes from --report-format and --report-path, and stdin is handy for testing a rule. dir with --log-opts is a distractor: log-opts applies to the git subcommand.

q: You are introducing gitleaks into a repo with 8 years of history. The first scan finds 45 old findings (all the secrets have already been revoked), and the team wants MRs to fail only on NEW secrets. What do you do?
options: Set allow_failure: true on the job
Disable the generic-api-key rule
Add --exit-code 0
Create a redacted baseline report and use --baseline-path in the pipeline
explain: --baseline-path ignores findings already in the baseline report, so the job fails only on new ones. allow_failure and --exit-code 0 disable the gate for everything, including new secrets, and turning off a rule doesn't distinguish old from new.

q: A developer says a pre-commit hook with gitleaks is enough and that a pipeline job isn't needed. What is the key counterargument?
options: The hook is slow and doesn't support .gitleaks.toml
The hook only works on Linux
The hook is on the developer's machine: it can be bypassed with git commit --no-verify or never installed, so you also need a control on the server
pre-commit can't call a binary, only Python scripts
explain: A local hook is a convenience, not a guaranteed control. Push protection and a mandatory pipeline job are on the server and don't depend on a laptop. The hook supports configuration, works on all platforms, and language: system calls any binary.

q: Which .pre-commit-config.yaml works in the lab without network access and scans only staged changes?
options:
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks
        name: gitleaks
        entry: gitleaks git --pre-commit --staged --redact
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.30.0
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks
        entry: gitleaks dir .
        language: python

hooks:
  pre-commit: gitleaks protect
explain: repo: local with language: system calls the installed gitleaks without downloading anything, and git --pre-commit --staged looks only at what goes into the commit. The official hook from GitHub needs network access for cloning, language: python would try to build an environment and dir scans the whole directory, and the fourth option isn't the pre-commit format.

q: tests/fixtures/ contains deliberately fake keys for tests, and gitleaks reports 12 findings every time. What is the most appropriate exception?
options: Add # gitleaks:allow at the end of every file
[[allowlists]] in .gitleaks.toml with paths = ['''tests/fixtures/.*'''] and a description of the reason
Run gitleaks with --exit-code 0
Disable [extend] useDefault
explain: A path allowlist is narrow, documented and goes through review via an MR. gitleaks:allow applies only to the line it is on, --exit-code 0 turns off the gate for everything, and disabling the built-in rules also removes real detection.

q: A developer on a GitLab Ultimate project with secret push protection enabled gets a push rejected because of a test token and pushes with git push -o secret_push_protection.skip_all. What is true?
options: The push goes through, the bypass is recorded as an audit event, and pipeline secret detection will still scan the commits if it's enabled
The push fails again because push protection can't be bypassed
The push goes through and leaves no trace anywhere
The push goes through, but GitLab automatically revokes the token
explain: Push protection can be bypassed with a push option or with [skip secret push protection] in the commit message, and every bypass is recorded in the audit log. Pipeline secret detection is a separate control. GitLab doesn't automatically revoke third-party tokens.

q: Order the layers of protection against secret leaks by the moment they act, earliest first.
options: Periodic (scheduled) scan of the entire history of all branches
pre-commit hook on the developer's machine
gitleaks job in the MR pipeline over the MR's commits
Push protection on the Git server
explain: The hook acts before the commit, push protection at push time, the MR job after the push in the pipeline, and the periodic scan later catches what slipped through or what new rules only now recognize.

q: The line 3f2c9a1…:config/settings.py:aws-access-token:4 was added to .gitleaksignore without a comment, and there is no ticket for revoking the key. What is the problem?
options: The fingerprint format is wrong; it must start with the rule name
.gitleaksignore applies only to gitleaks dir
The fingerprint must be in .gitleaks.toml
The exception was added without evidence that the secret was revoked and without a reason; the finding is hidden, and the key may still be active
explain: An exception should mean "handled": revoked, with a reason, date and incident number. The commit:file:rule:line format is correct for a git scan, .gitleaksignore also applies to history, and fingerprints go precisely in that file.

q: Order the steps for responding to the leaked AWS key from the kurs-shop history.
options: Rewrite history (git filter-repo) if needed and add the fingerprint to .gitleaksignore with the incident number
Deactivate the key
Review CloudTrail events for that AccessKeyId
Issue a new secret (or an OIDC role), move the services over and delete the old key
explain: Revocation (deactivation) always comes first, then rotation so the services keep working, investigation of the usage, and finally cleaning up history and documenting the exception. The investigation can run in parallel with rotation, but never before deactivation.

q: The key has been deactivated. What is the fastest way to see what was done with that key in the last 90 days?
options: aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id AKIA...
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=AKIA...
aws iam list-access-keys --user-name kurs-shop-ci
explain: lookup-events filtered by AccessKeyId returns management events from the CloudTrail event history (90 days). get-access-key-last-used gives only the last use, get-caller-identity shows your own identity, and list-access-keys only lists the keys.

q: The repo is private, has 60 active developers and 40 open MRs. The leaked Slack webhook has been revoked and replaced. What is a reasonable next step?
options: Rewrite history and force push no matter what, regardless of the consequences
Delete the repo and create a new one
Do nothing further; the finding will go away on its own
Don't rewrite history; add the fingerprint to .gitleaksignore with the incident number and revocation date, and introduce a hook and push protection
explain: A revoked secret is harmless, and rewriting history would change all hashes and break open MRs and local branches. A documented exception and prevention are more sensible. Without an exception, the periodic scan would keep reporting the same finding.

q: After git filter-repo --replace-text and a force push of all branches, gitleaks finds no secret in a fresh clone. What is still exposed?
options: Nothing: filter-repo removes the secret from the server and from all clones
Developers' old clones, forks, artifacts and runner caches, and on GitLab also the old objects until Repository cleanup / Remove blobs is run
Only tags, because filter-repo doesn't change them
Only the .gitleaksignore file
explain: Rewriting changes only the repo you push; copies outside it remain, and the server keeps old objects (e.g. via MR references) until it is cleaned up. filter-repo rewrites tags too. That's why revoking the secret is always mandatory.
